q: A photoreceptor is a receptor that is sensitive to:
x: Photoreceptors, such as the rods and cones of the retina, respond to light. Sound is detected by mechanoreceptors and dissolved chemicals by chemoreceptors.

q: In biology, a stimulus is best defined as:
o: A change in the internal or external environment that can be detected by a receptor
A nerve impulse travelling from the brain to a muscle
A chemical released at the end of an axon
The response made by a muscle or gland
x: A stimulus is any detectable change inside or outside the body. The response is made by an effector, and a chemical released at an axon ending is a neurotransmitter.

q: Receptors for touch, pressure, pain and temperature are present in large numbers in the:
x: The skin contains Meissner's and Pacinian corpuscles, free nerve endings for pain and thermoreceptors. The retina, cochlea and olfactory epithelium hold receptors for light, sound and smell.

q: The minimum strength of a stimulus that can make a receptor set up nerve impulses is called its:
x: A stimulus must reach the threshold strength before nerve impulses are produced. Weaker stimuli produce no impulse.

q: A microphone changes sound energy into electrical signals. A sensory receptor is compared to a microphone because both:
o: Amplify signals without changing their form
Change one form of energy into another
x: Both are transducers: they convert one form of energy into another. A receptor changes the energy of a stimulus into the electrical energy of nerve impulses.

q: In the skin, a thermoreceptor acts as a transducer that converts:
x: A thermoreceptor detects heat (temperature change) and converts it into nerve impulses. Receptors always produce impulses as their output, not the other way round.

q: When the layers of a Pacinian corpuscle are squeezed by firm pressure, the corpuscle transduces:
x: Pressure is mechanical energy; deforming the corpuscle sets up impulses in its nerve ending. That is why it is classed as a mechanoreceptor.

q: Which pairing of a receptor and the form of energy it transduces is correct?
x: Taste cells are chemoreceptors that respond to dissolved chemicals. Cones respond to light, cochlear hair cells to sound vibrations and thermoreceptors to heat.

q: Thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus of the brain monitor the:
o: Oxygen content of the cerebrospinal fluid
Temperature of the blood flowing through it
Pressure of blood in the carotid arteries
x: The hypothalamus contains thermoreceptors that sense blood temperature, which it uses to regulate body temperature. Blood pressure is sensed by baroreceptors in the arteries.

q: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus are stimulated mainly by a change in the:
o: Stretch of the urinary bladder wall
Solute concentration (osmotic pressure) of the blood
x: Osmoreceptors detect changes in the osmotic pressure (water and solute balance) of the blood. Bladder stretch is detected by mechanoreceptors.

q: The receptors of the olfactory epithelium and those of the taste buds belong to the same class because both respond to:
x: Smell and taste receptors are both chemoreceptors: they respond to molecules dissolved in mucus or saliva.

q: Receptors in muscles, tendons and joints that keep the brain informed about the position of body parts are called:
x: Proprioceptors, such as muscle spindles, signal the position and stretch of muscles and joints. Nociceptors detect pain and osmoreceptors detect blood concentration.

q: A person stops noticing a wristwatch soon after putting it on, although it still presses on the skin. This is mainly because the touch receptors:
o: Are destroyed by the continued pressure
Adapt, sending fewer impulses to an unchanging stimulus
Send their impulses only to the spinal cord
x: Many receptors adapt: with a constant stimulus their impulse frequency falls, so the sensation fades. The receptors are not damaged and still respond to any new change.

q: Sensory receptors in the body are built in different ways. Which description of their build is accurate?
o: All receptors are free nerve endings without any covering
Some are free nerve endings, while others are specialised cells or capsules linked to nerve endings
All receptors are separate cells with no contact with neurons
Receptors are found only in the special sense organs
x: Pain receptors are free nerve endings, Pacinian corpuscles are capsules around a nerve ending, and taste or rod cells are specialised cells that pass signals to neurons. Receptors also occur in skin, muscles and blood vessels.

q: Hair cells in the semicircular canals of the inner ear are stimulated by:
o: Changes in the temperature of the blood
x: The semicircular canals detect rotation of the head for balance; their hair cells are mechanoreceptors moved by the fluid inside. Sound is detected in the cochlea.

q: A person touches a hot iron and feels a sharp burning pain. The pain is first detected by:
o: Nociceptors, which are free nerve endings
Pacinian corpuscles deep in the dermis
Meissner's corpuscles in the dermal papillae
x: Pain arising from damaging heat is detected by nociceptors, which are free nerve endings. Meissner's and Pacinian corpuscles detect touch and pressure; baroreceptors lie in artery walls.

q: Which of the following is NOT a chemoreceptor?
x: A Pacinian corpuscle responds to pressure, so it is a mechanoreceptor. Smell, taste and carotid body cells all respond to chemicals.

q: Which sequence correctly shows the path from a stimulus to a response?
o: Stimulus → effector → motor neuron → CNS → sensory neuron → receptor
Stimulus → sensory neuron → receptor → CNS → effector → motor neuron
Stimulus → CNS → receptor → motor neuron → sensory neuron → effector
Stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → CNS → motor neuron → effector
x: The receptor detects the stimulus first and sends impulses along a sensory neuron to the CNS. A motor neuron then carries impulses to the effector.

q: Gentle pressure on a closed eye can make a person 'see' flashes of light. This shows that the sensation felt depends mainly on:
o: The form of energy in the stimulus
Which part of the brain receives the impulses
The strength of the pressure applied
The number of touch receptors in the eyelid
x: All receptors send the same kind of nerve impulse. Pressure that stimulates the retina sends impulses to the visual area, so the brain interprets them as light, whatever the stimulus was.

q: Baroreceptors in the walls of major arteries respond directly to changes in:
x: Baroreceptors are stretch-sensitive mechanoreceptors; a change in blood pressure changes how much the artery wall is stretched. Oxygen level is sensed by chemoreceptors.

q: Structurally, most thermoreceptors of the skin are:
o: Capsules of concentric connective tissue layers
x: Skin thermoreceptors are free nerve endings. Concentric capsules describe Pacinian corpuscles, rod-shaped cells are in the retina and hair cells are in the inner ear.

q: Which receptor is correctly paired with its location?
o: Pacinian corpuscles – outer layer of the epidermis
Olfactory receptor cells – roof of the nasal cavity
x: Olfactory cells lie in the epithelium at the roof of the nasal cavity. Pacinian corpuscles are deep in the dermis, taste cells are in taste buds and rods and cones are in the retina.

q: Colour vision in bright light depends on which photoreceptors?
x: Cones work in bright light and distinguish colours. Rods work in dim light and do not give colour vision.

q: During exercise, chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies detect a rise in blood carbon dioxide. The response that follows is:
o: A fall in both heart rate and breathing rate
An increase in the rate and depth of breathing
x: Impulses from these chemoreceptors stimulate the breathing centre, so breathing becomes faster and deeper to remove the extra carbon dioxide.

q: The olfactory receptor cells in the nose are themselves:
o: Capsules of connective tissue around nerve endings
Muscle cells that contract when stimulated
Neurons whose own axons carry impulses towards the brain
x: Olfactory receptors are modified neurons; their axons pass to the brain as the olfactory nerve. Mucus is made by other cells of the epithelium.

q: Unlike an action potential, the generator (receptor) potential produced in a receptor:
o: Is always of exactly the same size
Varies in size with the strength of the stimulus
Travels along the whole axon without change
Is produced only by stimuli above threshold
x: A generator potential is graded: a stronger stimulus gives a larger one. Only when it reaches threshold does it set up all-or-none action potentials in the sensory neuron.

q: When a stimulus acts on a receptor, the first change that leads to nerve impulses is:
o: Release of neurotransmitter from the receptor into the blood
A change in the permeability of the receptor membrane to ions
A rise in ATP production by the receptor's mitochondria
x: Transduction begins when the stimulus alters ion permeability of the receptor membrane, producing a generator potential. If this reaches threshold, impulses follow.

q: A typical neuron has:
o: Many axons and a single dendrite
One axon and one or more dendrites
Two axons joined at the cell body
x: A typical neuron has a single axon carrying impulses away from the cell body and one or more dendrites carrying them towards it.

q: The process of a neuron that carries impulses away from the cell body is the:
x: The axon conducts impulses away from the cell body. Dendrites carry them towards it; Nissl's granules and neurofibrils are structures inside the cytoplasm.

q: The cytoplasm inside an axon is called the:
x: The cytoplasm of an axon is axoplasm. Sarcoplasm is muscle-fibre cytoplasm and nucleoplasm is inside the nucleus.

q: The two properties most highly developed in neurons are:
x: Neurons are specialised to respond to stimuli (excitability) and carry impulses (conductivity). Contractility is the special property of muscle.

q: The cone-shaped region of the cell body from which the axon arises, where impulses usually start, is the:
x: The axon leaves the cell body at the axon hillock, where action potentials are usually triggered. Nodes of Ranvier are gaps in the myelin further along.

q: At its far end, the axon divides into fine terminal branches. Each branch ends in a swelling called the:
x: Axon terminals end in synaptic knobs (terminal buttons) that hold vesicles of neurotransmitter. The axon hillock is at the start of the axon, not its end.

q: A motor neuron, which has one axon and many dendrites arising from its cell body, is described as:
x: Many processes leaving the cell body make a neuron multipolar. A bipolar neuron has just one dendrite and one axon.

q: Bipolar neurons, with one dendrite and one axon on opposite sides of the cell body, are found in the:
o: Ventral horn of the spinal cord
x: Bipolar neurons occur in the retina (and in the olfactory epithelium). Ventral horn and motor cortex neurons are multipolar, and dorsal root ganglia hold unipolar sensory neurons.

q: Sensory neurons of spinal nerves have a single process leaving the cell body, which then splits into two branches. Such neurons are described as:
x: One process leaving the cell body defines a unipolar neuron; it divides into a peripheral branch from the receptor and a central branch into the spinal cord.

q: Compared with motor neurons, associative (relay) neurons usually have:
o: Short axons and link neurons inside the CNS
Very long axons that reach muscles
Cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia
Thick myelin sheaths made by Schwann cells
x: Associative neurons are short and connect sensory and motor neurons within the brain and spinal cord. Long axons reaching muscles belong to motor neurons.

q: Which type of neuron is the most numerous in the human nervous system?
x: The vast majority of neurons lie entirely in the brain and spinal cord as associative neurons, linking and processing signals.

q: The grey matter of the brain and spinal cord consists mainly of:
o: Neuron cell bodies, dendrites and non-myelinated fibres
x: Grey matter lacks much myelin; it is made of cell bodies, dendrites and non-myelinated fibres. White matter is mainly myelinated axons.

q: Which feature of a neuron allows it to carry signals quickly over long distances, such as from the spinal cord to the foot?
o: A long axon covered with a myelin sheath
A large nucleus in the cell body
Many Nissl's granules in the cell body
x: A long axon reaches distant effectors and its myelin sheath speeds conduction. Dendrites receive signals and Nissl's granules make proteins.

q: Cells of nervous tissue that support, protect and nourish neurons but do not conduct impulses are called:
x: Neuroglia, including Schwann cells, support neurons. Neurofibrils and Nissl's granules are structures inside neurons, not separate cells.

q: Damage to the brain is often permanent because mature neurons:
o: Normally do not divide to replace lost cells
x: Mature neurons do not undergo cell division, so lost neurons are not replaced. They do have a nucleus and make proteins actively.

q: Nissl's granules are found in the cell body of a neuron but not in its axon. Therefore proteins needed by the axon must be:
o: Made by ribosomes spread throughout the axon
Absorbed from tissue fluid around the axon
Made at the nodes of Ranvier
Made in the cell body and carried along the axon
x: Nissl's granules (rough ER and ribosomes) are the protein-making sites. Since the axon lacks them, its proteins are made in the cell body and transported down the axon.

q: The highly branched dendrites of a motor neuron are an advantage because they:
o: Insulate the cell body from ions
Store the ATP the neuron needs
Provide a large surface to receive signals from many other neurons
x: Branching gives a large area for synapses with many other neurons. Releasing transmitter onto muscle is done by the axon terminals.

q: Synaptic knobs contain many mitochondria. This is because the knobs need:
o: Oxygen to store in their vesicles
ATP for making and releasing neurotransmitter
x: Synthesis of transmitter and its release by exocytosis need energy, supplied as ATP by the mitochondria.

q: A cut peripheral nerve fibre can regrow, but a cut fibre in the spinal cord usually cannot. An important reason is that peripheral fibres have a:
o: Larger number of Nissl's granules in the axon
x: The neurilemma (Schwann cell sheath) of peripheral fibres guides and supports regrowth of a cut axon. Fibres in the CNS lack a neurilemma.

q: The ventral root of a spinal nerve contains mainly the axons of:
x: Motor axons leave the spinal cord through the ventral root. Sensory fibres enter through the dorsal root, whose ganglion holds their cell bodies.

q: The term 'nerve fibre' refers to:
o: A single axon or long dendrite with its covering sheaths
A bundle of many axons wrapped in connective tissue
The cell body of a neuron with its nucleus
A group of cell bodies outside the CNS
x: A nerve fibre is one long neuron process with its sheaths. A bundle of fibres is a nerve, and a group of cell bodies outside the CNS is a ganglion.

q: In a myelinated peripheral nerve fibre, the correct order of layers from the centre outwards is:
x: The Schwann cell wraps its membrane many times around the axon to form myelin; its outer layer with nucleus and cytoplasm is the neurilemma.

q: A neuron receives most of its incoming signals from other neurons at its:
x: Synapses from other neurons are mostly on the dendrites and cell body. Axon terminals pass signals on to the next cell.

q: The cell body of a neuron has a large nucleus with a prominent nucleolus and many Nissl's granules. These features show that the cell body is very active in:
x: A prominent nucleolus makes ribosomes, and Nissl's granules are rough ER with ribosomes: both point to active protein synthesis. Mature neurons do not divide.

q: Side branches given off along the length of an axon are called:
x: Collaterals are branches of the axon itself and conduct impulses away from the cell body. Dendrites are separate processes of the cell body.

q: The axon terminals of a motor neuron that supplies skeletal muscle end at:
o: Neuromuscular junctions on the muscle fibres
Nodes of Ranvier on the muscle fibres
x: A motor neuron passes its signal to skeletal muscle at neuromuscular junctions. Nodes of Ranvier are features of myelinated axons, not muscle.

q: Nodes of Ranvier are present only in:
o: The cell body of a neuron
x: Nodes of Ranvier are the gaps between segments of the myelin sheath, so they exist only where there is myelin.

q: A resting neuron is said to be polarised because:
o: The inside of its membrane is negative compared with the outside
Its Na+ channels are fully open
The inside of its membrane is positive compared with the outside
x: At rest there is a charge difference across the membrane, with the inside negative (about -70 mV). The inside becomes positive only briefly during an action potential.

q: The level to which the membrane must be depolarised to trigger an action potential is called the:
x: Once depolarisation reaches the threshold potential, an action potential fires. The resting potential is the starting value at rest.

q: The resting membrane potential of a neuron is a potential difference across its:
x: The resting potential exists across the plasma membrane because of the unequal distribution of ions inside and outside the cell.

q: The sodium–potassium pump moves ions across the neuron membrane by:
x: The pump moves Na+ and K+ against their concentration gradients, which needs energy from ATP: this is active transport.

q: The Na+ channels that open when the axon membrane is depolarised to threshold are called:
x: These channels open in response to a change in membrane voltage. Ligand-gated channels open when a chemical such as a neurotransmitter binds.

q: During depolarisation, Na+ ions enter the axon by:
o: Active transport by the sodium–potassium pump
Diffusion down their concentration and electrical gradients through open channels
x: Na+ is more concentrated outside and the inside is negative, so Na+ diffuses in passively once its channels open. The pump moves Na+ outwards, not in.

q: During repolarisation of the axon membrane, the voltage-gated Na+ channels:
o: Allow K+ to enter the axon
x: At the peak the Na+ channels close and K+ channels open; K+ leaving the axon brings the potential back to negative.

q: At rest, K+ ions slowly leave the neuron mainly through:
o: Potassium leak channels that stay open
x: Leak channels let K+ diffuse out at rest, which helps make the inside negative. The pump moves K+ inwards, not out.

q: The sodium–potassium pump helps keep the inside of a resting neuron negative because it:
o: Moves more positive charges out than it brings in
Brings negative chloride ions into the cell
Moves equal numbers of ions in each direction
Pumps protein anions out of the cell
x: By moving three Na+ out for every two K+ in, the pump removes more positive charge than it adds. Protein anions stay inside the cell.

q: Which statement correctly describes the ion distribution of a resting neuron?
o: Na+ is more concentrated inside and K+ outside
Na+ and K+ are equally concentrated on both sides
K+ is more concentrated inside and Na+ is more concentrated outside
Both Na+ and K+ are more concentrated inside
x: The pump keeps Na+ high outside and K+ high inside. These gradients make the resting potential and action potential possible.

q: An action potential spreads along a non-myelinated axon because:
o: Neurotransmitter is released at every point along the axon
The axon membrane contracts in waves
Local currents from the depolarised region bring the next part of the membrane to threshold
The sodium–potassium pump pushes the impulse forward
x: Positive charge flows from the active region to the neighbouring resting region, depolarising it to threshold, so a new action potential arises there.

q: A single action potential at one point of an axon lasts about:
x: Depolarisation and repolarisation together take only about one to two milliseconds at any one point of the membrane.

q: The neurotransmitter released at the junctions between motor neurons and skeletal muscle fibres is:
x: Motor neurons are cholinergic: they release acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions. Noradrenaline is released by most sympathetic endings.

q: The enzyme acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft breaks acetylcholine down into:
x: Acetylcholinesterase hydrolyses acetylcholine to choline and acetate, ending its action. The choline is taken back into the knob and reused.

q: When acetylcholine binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane of a neuron, the immediate effect is that:
o: Synaptic vesicles fuse with the postsynaptic membrane
Ion channels open, Na+ enters and the membrane depolarises
x: The receptors are linked to ion channels; when they open, Na+ enters and depolarises the postsynaptic membrane. Ca2+ entry into the knob happens earlier, before release.

q: A weak stimulus depolarises a small patch of axon membrane but does not reach threshold. The result is:
o: A small action potential that travels more slowly
A full action potential that travels only halfway
A burst of several small impulses
A small local change that fades away without an impulse
x: Below threshold there is only a small local depolarisation that dies away. Action potentials are all-or-none and do not come in small sizes.

q: The refractory period of a neuron sets an upper limit on the:
o: Number of impulses it can carry each second
x: A new action potential cannot start until the refractory period ends, so only a limited number of impulses can pass each second.

q: A second strong stimulus is applied to a point on an axon while the first action potential there is still at its peak. The second stimulus:
o: Immediately produces a second action potential of the same size
Produces no new action potential, because that region is in the absolute refractory period
Makes the first impulse travel backwards
x: During the absolute refractory period no stimulus, however strong, can start another action potential, because the Na+ channels cannot reopen yet.

q: An impulse travelling along an axon does not spread back over the part it has just passed because:
o: That part of the membrane is still in its refractory period
Myelin always blocks ions behind the impulse
Behind the impulse the membrane stays permanently depolarised
The Na+ concentration behind the impulse falls to zero
x: The membrane just behind the action potential is refractory, so local currents can only trigger the resting membrane ahead. This keeps conduction one-way along the axon.

q: Besides being faster, saltatory conduction in myelinated fibres saves energy because:
o: Myelinated neurons never need any ATP
Ions cross the membrane only at the nodes, so the pump has less to restore
Myelinated fibres have no sodium–potassium pumps
x: With ion flow limited to the nodes, fewer Na+ and K+ ions move per impulse, so less ATP is spent by the pump restoring the gradients. Pumps and ATP are still needed.

q: Unlike an electric current in a long wire, a nerve impulse does not get weaker as it travels along an axon because:
o: The myelin sheath adds energy to it
Neurotransmitter boosts it at every node
The axon is a perfect electrical conductor
It is regenerated at each successive part of the membrane
x: Each region of membrane produces its own full-size action potential, so the impulse is renewed as it goes. The axoplasm is actually a poor conductor.

q: A puffer-fish toxin blocks the voltage-gated Na+ channels of axons. The direct effect on these axons is that they:
x: Depolarisation needs the inflow of Na+ through voltage-gated channels. With them blocked, threshold cannot lead to an action potential, so conduction stops.

q: A drug blocks the voltage-gated K+ channels of an axon but not its Na+ channels. The action potentials produced would show:
o: A faster return to the resting potential
x: Depolarisation by Na+ still occurs, but repolarisation depends on K+ leaving through these channels, so it is slowed and the action potential lasts longer.

q: The brief hyperpolarisation at the end of an action potential occurs because:
o: Na+ channels open a second time
K+ channels close slowly, so slightly too much K+ leaves
Ca2+ ions flood into the axon
x: The voltage-gated K+ channels stay open a little after the resting value is reached, so extra K+ leaves and the inside becomes briefly more negative.

q: Immediately after one action potential, the concentrations of Na+ and K+ inside the axon have:
o: Reversed, with more Na+ than K+ inside
Changed only very slightly, because few ions cross the membrane
x: Only a tiny fraction of the ions cross during one impulse, which is enough to change the voltage but barely alters concentrations. The pump later restores them.

q: Thick axons conduct impulses faster than thin ones mainly because:
o: The wider axoplasm offers less resistance to the local currents
Their membranes have no ion channels
x: A larger diameter lowers the internal resistance, so local currents spread further and faster, bringing the next region to threshold sooner.

q: Sneezing when dust irritates the lining of the nose is a reflex whose centre lies in the brainstem. It is classified as a:
x: Reflexes integrated in the brain (here the brainstem) and using cranial nerves are cranial reflexes. Sneezing is inborn, so it is not a conditioned reflex, and it happens without a conscious decision.

q: When reflexes are divided into monosynaptic and polysynaptic types, the basis of the division is the:
o: Part of the central nervous system where the reflex is integrated
Number of synapses between neurons in the reflex arc
Whether the reflex is inborn or learned
Type of effector that gives the response
x: Monosynaptic arcs have one synapse (sensory neuron directly to motor neuron); polysynaptic arcs have interneurons and so more synapses. The spinal/cranial division depends on the centre, and conditioned/unconditioned on learning.

q: Shedding tears when the eyes are irritated by vapour from a freshly cut onion is an example of:
x: Tear secretion in response to an irritant is inborn and needs no learning, so it is an unconditioned reflex. Conditioned reflexes and habits are acquired through experience.

q: After training was complete, the sound of the bell in Pavlov's work with dogs served as the:
x: The bell produces salivation only after it has been repeatedly paired with food, so it is a conditioned stimulus. Food is the unconditioned stimulus, and salivation to the bell is the conditioned response.

q: Before any training began, the bell in Pavlov's experiment was:
o: An unconditioned stimulus that caused salivation
A neutral stimulus that caused no salivation
A conditioned stimulus that caused salivation
A reflex centre in the dog's brain
x: At first the bell had nothing to do with feeding and produced no salivation, so it was neutral. Only after repeated pairing with food did it become a conditioned stimulus.

q: A child who has had several painful injections starts crying as soon as she sees a syringe. This response is:
x: The sight of a syringe causes crying only because it has become linked with pain through past experience, so the response is learned: a conditioned reflex. A newborn would not respond this way.

q: The ankle-jerk reflex, in which tapping the Achilles tendon makes the calf muscle contract, is classified as a:
x: Like the knee jerk, the ankle jerk is a stretch reflex: the sensory neuron synapses directly with the motor neuron in the spinal cord. It is inborn, so it is not conditioned.

q: Blinking, coughing and the pupil reflex belong to one group of reflexes. What is true of this group?
o: They are all learned through experience after birth
They are integrated in the grey matter of the spinal cord
Their centres lie in the brain and their pathways use cranial nerves
x: These are cranial reflexes: they are integrated in the brain and use cranial nerves. They are inborn, not learned, and many have interneurons, so they are not always monosynaptic.

q: A frog whose brain has been destroyed still pulls its leg away when the foot is pinched. This shows that reflexes integrated in the spinal cord:
o: Must first be learned through training
Can occur without the brain taking part
Use cranial nerves for their pathways
Need the animal to be conscious
x: With the brain destroyed, only the spinal cord can link the sensory and motor neurons, yet the leg still withdraws. So spinal reflexes are organised in the spinal cord and need no brain or consciousness; they use spinal nerves.

q: Which pair of responses are BOTH unconditioned reflexes?
o: The knee jerk and a dog salivating at a dinner bell
Coughing and a child crying at the sight of a syringe
Blinking and stopping a car at a red signal
x: Sneezing and the knee jerk are inborn and need no learning. Salivating at a bell, fearing a syringe and stopping at a red signal are all learned through experience, so each wrong pair contains one conditioned response.

q: Which reflex is polysynaptic?
o: Withdrawing the foot after stepping on a thorn
The stretch reflex of the calf muscle
x: Withdrawal reflexes have at least one interneuron between the sensory and motor neurons, so they are polysynaptic. The knee jerk, ankle jerk and other stretch reflexes are monosynaptic.

q: Conditioned reflexes are established mainly through:
o: The growth of new spinal nerves
Repeated pairing of a new stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus
A single exposure to a stimulus without any reinforcement
x: A conditioned reflex forms when a neutral stimulus is repeatedly given together with an unconditioned stimulus, as with the bell and food. It is acquired, not inherited, and needs repetition.

q: Which statement correctly compares unconditioned and conditioned reflexes?
o: Conditioned reflexes are inherited, while unconditioned reflexes are learned
Unconditioned reflexes are similar in all members of a species, while conditioned reflexes differ between individuals
Unconditioned reflexes need training to form, while conditioned reflexes do not
Both types are permanent and can never fade
x: Unconditioned reflexes are inborn and common to the whole species. Conditioned reflexes depend on each individual's experience, so they differ from person to person and can fade if not reinforced.

q: In a reflex arc, the sensory neuron synapses with a single interneuron, which synapses with the motor neuron. How many synapses between neurons does this arc have?
x: There is one synapse from sensory neuron to interneuron and one from interneuron to motor neuron, giving two. This makes it a polysynaptic reflex; a monosynaptic arc would have only one.

q: Which feature distinguishes a reflex action from a voluntary action?
o: A reflex does not need a conscious decision before the response
A reflex always uses a gland as the effector
A reflex always involves the cerebral cortex
A reflex is slower than a voluntary action
x: Reflexes are automatic and involuntary: the response is produced without waiting for a conscious decision. They are usually faster than voluntary actions and can use muscles or glands.

q: Coughing, sneezing and blinking are grouped together because all three are:
o: Cranial reflexes with their centres in the brain
Spinal reflexes with their centres in the spinal cord
x: All three are inborn reflexes integrated in the brainstem and using cranial nerves, so they are cranial reflexes. They are not learned, and they are not stretch reflexes.

q: A withdrawal reflex arc with interneurons, compared with the knee-jerk arc, must have:
o: Fewer synapses and so a faster response
No synapses inside the spinal cord
More synapses and so a longer delay
Its centre in the brain instead of the spinal cord
x: Each interneuron adds a synapse, and each synapse adds a short delay, so the polysynaptic withdrawal arc is slower than the monosynaptic knee jerk. Both are spinal reflexes.

q: A reflex arc contains a sensory neuron, a chain of three interneurons and a motor neuron. How many synapses between neurons are present in this arc?
x: Five neurons joined end to end have four junctions between them: sensory to first interneuron, two between interneurons, and last interneuron to motor neuron. The junction with the effector is not a synapse between neurons.

q: A man once stung by a bee now flinches whenever he hears buzzing nearby. He also blinks when a bee touches his eyelid. The flinch and the blink are, respectively:
x: Flinching at the buzzing sound is learned from the earlier sting, so it is conditioned. Blinking when the eyelid is touched is inborn, so it is unconditioned.

q: The pupil reflex to bright light differs from the knee-jerk reflex in that the pupil reflex is:
o: Cranial and polysynaptic, while the knee jerk is spinal and monosynaptic
Spinal and monosynaptic, while the knee jerk is cranial and polysynaptic
Conditioned, while the knee jerk is unconditioned
Cranial and monosynaptic, while the knee jerk is spinal and polysynaptic
x: The pupil reflex is integrated in the midbrain and passes through several neurons, so it is cranial and polysynaptic. The knee jerk is a spinal stretch reflex with one synapse. Both are unconditioned.

q: In a reflex arc, the part of the central nervous system that receives the sensory impulse and sends out the motor impulse acts as the:
x: The brain or spinal cord acts as the integrating (coordinating) centre, linking the incoming sensory impulse to an outgoing motor impulse. The receptor detects the stimulus and the effector responds.

q: When the effector of a reflex arc is a gland, the response it produces is:
x: Glands respond by secreting, for example saliva or tears. Contraction is the response of a muscle effector, and detecting a stimulus is the job of the receptor.

q: The sensory neuron of a reflex arc is also called the:
x: The sensory neuron carries impulses towards the CNS, so it is afferent. The motor neuron is efferent, and the relay neuron is the interneuron inside the CNS.

q: In the blinking reflex that follows a touch on the cornea, the effector is the:
x: The response is closing of the eyelid, so the effector is the eyelid muscle. The corneal nerve endings are the receptors, and the iris muscle is the effector of the pupil reflex, not of blinking.

q: In the coughing reflex, the receptors that are stimulated lie in the:
o: Lining of the larynx and trachea
x: Coughing begins when irritants stimulate receptors in the lining of the air passages such as the larynx and trachea. The diaphragm and other breathing muscles are effectors, not receptors.

q: In the reflex in which food on the tongue causes saliva to flow, the receptors are the:
o: Stretch receptors in the jaw muscles
Taste receptors in the taste buds
x: Chemicals in the food stimulate the taste receptors (chemoreceptors) of the taste buds, which start the impulse. The salivary glands are the effectors, and motor neurons carry the outgoing impulse.

q: Bright light makes the pupil narrow. Which cells detect the light and start this reflex?
x: Light is detected by the rods and cones of the retina, which start the impulse. The circular muscles of the iris are the effector; the cornea and lens only focus light.

q: The dorsal root ganglion, a small swelling on the dorsal root of each spinal nerve, is part of the reflex pathway. It contains the:
o: Synapses between sensory and motor neurons
x: The dorsal root ganglion holds the cell bodies of the sensory (afferent) neurons. Motor neuron cell bodies, interneurons and the synapses of the arc all lie in the grey matter of the spinal cord.

q: At the junction between the motor neuron of a spinal reflex and the skeletal muscle it supplies, the neurotransmitter released is:
x: Motor neurons release acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, which makes the skeletal muscle fibre contract. Noradrenaline is released by sympathetic nerve endings, not at skeletal muscle.

q: Nerve fibres that carry information about a spinal reflex up to the brain run in the:
o: Ventral roots of the spinal nerves
White matter of the spinal cord
Central canal of the spinal cord
x: Long tracts of myelinated fibres in the white matter carry impulses up and down the spinal cord, letting the brain learn of the stimulus. Ventral roots carry motor fibres out, and the central canal holds cerebrospinal fluid.

q: A person keeps holding a hot dish instead of dropping it, overriding the withdrawal reflex. This is possible because:
o: Impulses from the brain can inhibit the motor neurons of the reflex arc
The heat receptors in the skin stop responding
The sensory neuron is disconnected from the spinal cord
The effector muscle loses its nerve supply
x: Descending fibres from the brain synapse on the motor neurons in the spinal cord and can inhibit them, so a reflex can be overridden. The receptors and sensory neurons still work, which is why the heat is felt.

q: Which component of a spinal reflex arc is NOT part of the nervous system?
x: The effector is a muscle (or gland) that carries out the response; it is not nervous tissue. The sensory, inter- and motor neurons are all parts of the nervous system.

q: Which structure carries both the sensory and the motor fibres of a spinal reflex arc between the spinal cord and a limb?
o: The spinal nerve formed where the dorsal and ventral roots join
x: The dorsal root carries only sensory fibres and the ventral root only motor fibres. They join to form the spinal nerve, which is a mixed nerve carrying both to and from the limb.

q: In the reflex in which the pupil narrows in bright light, impulses from the receptors travel to the brain along the:
x: The receptors are in the retina, and their impulses leave the eye in the optic nerve. This is a cranial reflex, so spinal nerves are not involved.

q: The integrating centre of the reflex that narrows the pupil in bright light lies in the:
x: The pupil reflex is coordinated in the midbrain, which contains centres for visual reflexes. The occipital lobe is where light is consciously seen, but the reflex does not need it.

q: When dust enters the eye, tears flow to wash it out. In this reflex the effector is the:
x: Tears are secreted by the lacrimal gland, which is the effector here. The retina contains photoreceptors, and the iris muscle is the effector of the pupil reflex.

q: A drug blocks the acetylcholine receptors on skeletal muscle fibres. In a spinal reflex arc, which step would fail?
o: Detection of the stimulus by the receptor
Transmission from sensory neuron to interneuron
x: Acetylcholine released by the motor neuron cannot act on the muscle, so the effector does not contract. The receptor, sensory neuron and synapses within the spinal cord are not affected by blocking the muscle's receptors.

q: Only the interneurons in one segment of the spinal cord are destroyed; sensory and motor neurons survive. Which reflex of that segment would still work?
o: A withdrawal reflex from a painful stimulus
None of the reflexes of that segment
A stretch reflex such as a tendon jerk
x: Stretch reflexes are monosynaptic: the sensory neuron synapses directly with the motor neuron, so no interneuron is needed. Withdrawal reflexes depend on interneurons and would fail.

q: A spinal nerve supplying part of the leg is cut beyond the point where its dorsal and ventral roots join. In the area it supplies:
o: Only sensation is lost, while reflexes remain
Sensation, reflexes and voluntary movement are all lost
Only voluntary movement is lost, while sensation remains
Sensation remains, but reflexes are lost
x: Beyond the junction of the roots the spinal nerve is mixed, carrying both sensory and motor fibres. Cutting it stops impulses in both directions, so sensation, reflexes and voluntary movement are all lost.

q: In a withdrawal reflex with one interneuron, which pair of events BOTH take place inside the central nervous system?
o: Generation of the impulse in the receptor, and transmission at the neuromuscular junction
Contraction of the effector, and transmission at the neuromuscular junction
Generation of the impulse in the receptor, and transmission from sensory neuron to interneuron
Transmission from sensory neuron to interneuron, and from interneuron to motor neuron
x: Both synapses involving the interneuron lie in the grey matter of the spinal cord. The receptor lies in the skin, and the neuromuscular junction and effector are in the limb, outside the CNS.

q: The raised ridges on the folded surface of the cerebral cortex are called:
x: The cortex is folded into ridges called gyri, separated by grooves called sulci. Ventricles are cavities inside the brain, and meninges are its covering membranes.

q: Cerebrospinal fluid is produced mainly by the:
x: Networks of capillaries called choroid plexuses, lining the ventricles, secrete cerebrospinal fluid. The dura mater is a protective membrane and the corpus callosum is a band of nerve fibres.

q: Which of the following is a lobe of each cerebral hemisphere?
x: Each cerebral hemisphere has frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes. The pons is part of the brainstem, the vermis joins the cerebellar hemispheres, and the thalamus lies deep in the forebrain.

q: The thalamus and hypothalamus together make up the part of the forebrain called the:
x: The diencephalon is the part of the forebrain made of the thalamus and hypothalamus. The telencephalon forms the cerebrum, and the mesencephalon is the midbrain.

q: In the developing embryo, the part that becomes the hindbrain is called the:
x: The three embryonic divisions are the prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain) and rhombencephalon (hindbrain). The diencephalon is a part of the forebrain.

q: The pituitary gland hangs below the brain, attached by a stalk to the:
x: The pituitary is joined by a short stalk to the hypothalamus at the base of the forebrain. This close link lets the hypothalamus control the pituitary.

q: The pia mater is best described as:
o: A tough outer membrane lying next to the skull
A thin, delicate membrane closely attached to the surface of the brain
A layer of white matter beneath the cortex
x: The pia mater is the innermost meninx, thin and rich in blood vessels, following every fold of the brain. The tough outer layer is the dura mater and the web-like middle layer is the arachnoid.

q: The corpus callosum is made up mainly of:
x: The corpus callosum is a broad band of white matter: myelinated axons that cross between the two hemispheres. Neuron cell bodies make up grey matter.

q: The medulla oblongata leaves the skull and continues as the spinal cord through the:
x: The foramen magnum is the large opening in the base of the skull where the medulla becomes the spinal cord. The central sulcus and longitudinal fissure are grooves of the cerebrum.

q: How many ventricles are there in the human brain?
x: There are two lateral ventricles (one in each cerebral hemisphere), a third ventricle in the diencephalon and a fourth ventricle in the hindbrain, four in all.

q: In a section through the cerebellum, the branching, tree-like pattern of white matter is called the:
x: The white matter of the cerebellum branches like a tree inside the grey cortex and is called the arbor vitae ('tree of life'). The corpus callosum joins the cerebral hemispheres.

q: The pons gets its name, meaning 'bridge', because it:
o: Contains fibres linking the medulla, cerebellum and higher parts of the brain
Joins the left and right cerebral hemispheres
Joins the brain to the skull
Joins the pituitary gland to the hypothalamus
x: The pons is a bulge of the brainstem full of nerve fibres that bridge the medulla, the cerebellum and the parts above. The cerebral hemispheres are joined by the corpus callosum, not the pons.

q: On the back (dorsal side) of the midbrain are four rounded swellings called the:
x: The corpora quadrigemina are four small swellings on the roof of the midbrain, linked with visual and auditory reflexes. Olfactory bulbs belong to the forebrain.

q: Which structure lies directly above the hypothalamus in the forebrain?
x: The thalamus lies just above the hypothalamus; both form the diencephalon. The pons, cerebellum and medulla are hindbrain parts lying lower down.

q: The olfactory bulbs, which receive impulses from the smell receptors of the nose, are part of the:
x: The olfactory bulbs project forward from the underside of the cerebrum and belong to the forebrain. The midbrain and hindbrain lie behind and below.

q: The dura mater is the:
o: Innermost meninx attached to the brain surface
Tough, outermost meninx lying next to the skull
x: The dura mater is the thick, tough outer layer of the meninges. The arachnoid is the web-like middle layer and the pia mater is the thin inner layer on the brain surface.

q: The pineal gland is a small structure that belongs to the:
x: The pineal gland arises from the roof of the diencephalon, which is part of the forebrain. The cerebellum and medulla oblongata belong to the hindbrain.

q: A cross-section of part of the central nervous system shows white matter on the outside and an H-shaped area of grey matter around a narrow central canal. The section is from the:
x: In the spinal cord grey matter is central and H-shaped, with white matter around it. In the cerebrum and cerebellum the arrangement is the reverse: an outer grey cortex over inner white matter.

q: Which structure is part of the forebrain but NOT part of the cerebrum?
x: The forebrain includes the cerebrum and the diencephalon. The hypothalamus belongs to the diencephalon, while the frontal lobe, cortex and corpus callosum are all parts of the cerebrum.

q: Which statement about the cerebellum is correct?
o: It is part of the brainstem, lying between the midbrain and the pons
It belongs to the forebrain and is joined to the cerebrum by the corpus callosum
It belongs to the hindbrain, has a folded grey cortex, and is not part of the brainstem
It has white matter on the outside and grey matter inside
x: The cerebellum is a hindbrain part behind the pons and medulla, with a folded grey cortex over white matter. The brainstem is only the midbrain, pons and medulla.

q: The vasomotor centre, which controls the diameter of blood vessels and so helps regulate blood pressure, lies in the:
x: The medulla contains vital centres for heartbeat, breathing and blood vessel diameter (vasomotor centre). The cerebellum coordinates movement and the occipital lobe deals with vision.

q: Keeping balance while riding a bicycle and making the movements smooth depend mainly on the:
x: The cerebellum coordinates muscle activity, keeping movements smooth and the body balanced. The hypothalamus regulates internal conditions such as temperature.

q: Which part of the brain is the main control centre of the autonomic nervous system?
x: The hypothalamus controls the autonomic nervous system and so regulates involuntary activities of internal organs. The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement and the corpus callosum links the hemispheres.

q: Releasing hormones made by the hypothalamus act directly on the:
x: Hypothalamic releasing hormones travel in blood vessels to the anterior pituitary and control its secretions. The posterior pituitary instead stores hormones made by the hypothalamus itself.

q: To keep the body balanced, the cerebellum receives impulses from the:
o: Pain receptors of the skin only
Inner ear and stretch receptors in muscles and joints
x: The cerebellum uses information from the balance organs of the inner ear and from receptors in muscles and joints about body position. The cochlea is concerned with hearing, not balance.

q: A man's eyes and optic nerves are healthy, but after an injury to the back of his cerebrum he cannot see. The damaged part is the:
x: Visual impulses are interpreted in the visual area of the occipital lobe at the back of the cerebrum. If it is damaged, the person cannot see even though the eyes work.

q: A person in a very cold room begins to shiver. The brain centre that detects the fall in blood temperature and starts shivering is the:
x: The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat: it senses blood temperature and triggers responses such as shivering. The thalamus relays sensory impulses to the cortex.

q: The association areas of the cerebral cortex function to:
o: Interpret sensory information and link it with memory and motor responses
Directly control the rate of heartbeat
Relay impulses from the spinal cord to the cerebellum
x: Association areas analyse and combine information from the sensory areas, relate it to past experience and help plan responses. Heart rate is controlled by the medulla.

q: Impulses from touch receptors in the hand are passed on in which part of the forebrain before reaching the sensory area of the cortex?
x: Sensory impulses from the body are relayed in the thalamus, which passes them to the sensory area of the parietal lobe. The hypothalamus regulates internal conditions.

q: In most people, the areas controlling speech and language are found mainly in the:
x: In most people the language areas (for producing and understanding speech) lie in the left cerebral hemisphere. The cerebellum and medulla are not language centres.

q: Which pair of functions are BOTH controlled by centres in the medulla oblongata?
o: Body temperature and rate of breathing
Rate of breathing and blood pressure
x: The medulla contains the respiratory, cardiac and vasomotor centres. Balance is a cerebellum function, body temperature a hypothalamus function and vision an occipital lobe function.

q: The midbrain acts mainly as a:
o: Centre for controlling heartbeat and breathing
Relay and reflex centre for visual and auditory impulses
x: The midbrain relays visual and auditory information and coordinates reflexes such as the pupil reflex. Heartbeat and breathing are medulla functions, and intelligence belongs to the cerebrum.

q: Which function belongs to the cerebrum and NOT to the cerebellum?
o: Conscious perception of sensations such as pain
x: Sensations become conscious in the sensory areas of the cerebral cortex. Posture, balance and smooth coordination of movements are the work of the cerebellum.

q: A woman's ears and auditory nerves work normally, but after a stroke damaging both temporal lobes she cannot hear. This is because the temporal lobes contain the:
x: Sound impulses are interpreted in the auditory area of the temporal lobes, so damage there causes deafness even with normal ears. The visual area is in the occipital lobe and the motor area in the frontal lobe.

q: Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus but released from the posterior pituitary. It reaches the posterior pituitary by:
o: Being carried in the blood of the general circulation
Travelling down the axons of neurosecretory cells
x: Neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus send their axons down the pituitary stalk, and hormones such as oxytocin travel along them to be stored and released. This is a nervous link, not a general blood route.

q: Which statement about the functions of the brainstem is correct?
o: It is the main centre of intelligence and memory
It controls vital functions such as breathing and heartbeat and carries tracts between spinal cord and brain
It is responsible for the conscious perception of vision and hearing
It is the main centre for balance and posture
x: The brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla) contains vital centres and the nerve tracts linking the spinal cord with higher parts. Intelligence and conscious perception belong to the cerebrum, balance to the cerebellum.

q: Damage to the hypothalamus stops the production of antidiuretic hormone. Which effect is most likely?
o: Small volumes of very concentrated urine
Inability to see in bright light
Large volumes of dilute urine and strong thirst
x: Antidiuretic hormone from the hypothalamus makes the kidneys reabsorb water. Without it, much water is lost as dilute urine and the person becomes very thirsty. Balance and vision depend on other brain parts.

q: Impulses of which sense reach the cerebral cortex WITHOUT first being relayed in the thalamus?
x: The thalamus relays almost all sensory impulses to the cortex, including vision, hearing and touch. Smell is the exception: olfactory impulses pass from the olfactory bulbs directly to the cortex.

q: After severe damage to the cerebral cortex, a patient is unconscious, yet breathes normally and has a regular heartbeat. This is because:
o: The cerebellum has taken over the control of breathing
The cerebral cortex is the only centre for breathing and heartbeat
The breathing and heart centres in the medulla oblongata are still working
The thalamus controls breathing and heartbeat
x: Breathing and heart rate are controlled by centres in the medulla oblongata, not by the cortex. As long as the medulla is intact these vital functions continue, even when consciousness is lost.
